title: Augmenting large language models with chemistry tools
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem that large language models (LLMs) such as GPT-4 can be useful in scientific domains but often struggle with chemistry-specific reasoning, factuality, and access to up-to-date external knowledge. The authors propose ChemCrow, an LLM-powered chemistry agent that combines GPT-4 with a set of 18 expert-designed chemistry tools to support planning, search, safety checks, synthesis execution, and data analysis.

The intervention studied is not an educational intervention but a chemistry automation system. ChemCrow can invoke tools for web and literature search, molecular lookup and manipulation, reaction prediction, retrosynthesis, safety screening, and robotic synthesis execution. The paper demonstrates the system on several chemistry use cases, including planning and executing syntheses of DEET and thiourea organocatalysts, as well as a human–AI collaboration workflow in which ChemCrow helped clean data, train a model, and suggest a chromophore for synthesis.

The context is expert chemistry research using GPT-4, external software, and a cloud-connected robotic synthesis platform, with evaluation against tool-less GPT-4 and expert human judgments. The main conclusion is that tool augmentation substantially improves chemical factuality, task completion, and usefulness relative to GPT-4 alone, especially on more complex tasks. The paper also argues that human expert evaluation is more reliable than LLM-based evaluation for scientific tasks requiring factual correctness. No education-related population, grades 6–8 mathematics intervention, or classroom study is reported; the closest comparator evidence is the paper’s direct comparison of ChemCrow versus GPT-4 on chemistry tasks.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed empirical paper, but it is not an education study and does not evaluate a K-12 intervention or student learning design. The evidence is methodologically stronger than opinion/grey literature, but it has no direct relevance to the requested grades 6–8 ChatGPT mathematics search target.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational impact is demonstrated here. The paper concerns chemistry-agent automation, not classroom mathematics instruction, so it provides no impact evidence for the requested population or outcome.

interventions.use_case: ChemCrow, a GPT-4-based chemistry agent that uses tool-augmented conversation to plan, execute, and validate chemistry tasks such as synthesis planning, reaction prediction, safety checking, and literature/web search.

finding.finding_summary: The paper shows that ChemCrow improves task completion and chemical factuality relative to tool-less GPT-4 on chemistry tasks. In expert evaluation across 14 tasks (n=14 task-level comparisons; evaluators n=4), ChemCrow was preferred for chemical accuracy, reasoning, and completeness, and it successfully autonomously executed syntheses of DEET and three thiourea organocatalysts plus a chromophore-design workflow.
finding.measure: Expert ratings of chemical accuracy, quality of reasoning, and task completion; successful autonomous synthesis/execution on RoboRXN
